solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Relative is taken aback by gaudy jewellery

indicators.note: taken back, so the word is set down backwards

parts.note: IS written backwards
bling = flashy jewellery

explanation.surface: A family member recoils at someone's flashy jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: The little word 'is' looks like the verb of the sentence, but it is the raw material, turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother or sister is a close relative by birth.

clue.text: Criticising nerds is routine for soldiers?

definitions.meaning: squares are uncool, conventional people, and bashing is criticising: read literally, attacking squares
British military slang for parade-ground drill

explanation.surface: Picking on geeks is supposedly what soldiers do every day.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the jokey first reading. Square-bashing is British forces slang for marching drill on the parade square.
explanation.definitionFit: Square-bashing is the drill soldiers practise, and taken word by word it is bashing squares.

clue.text: Book reviewer's conclusion — it illuminated some works in English

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for book

indicators.note: the conclusion of a word is its final letter

parts.note: last letter of reviewer
used as it stands
lit = illuminated

explanation.surface: A critic's verdict that a book shed light on some English works.
explanation.walkthrough: Brit lit is informal, school-style shorthand for British literature. The dash makes 'it illuminated' look like part of the review.
explanation.definitionFit: Brit lit is British literature, a body of works in English.

clue.text: Bond kind of sarcastic after offing Goldfinger, finally?

indicators.note: offing means killing off, so once the letter is removed the rest remains

parts.note: ironic remarks are sarcastic ones

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of Goldfinger

parts.note: the last letter of Goldfinger

explanation.surface: A Bond film fan wonders whether a quip after Goldfinger's death was sarcastic, as in the 1964 James Bond film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives R, the last letter of Goldfinger, and 'after offing' takes it out of IRONIC. Bond is the chemical link, not James Bond.
explanation.definitionFit: An ionic bond is a chemical link formed by attraction between charged atoms, so ionic is a kind of bond.

clue.text: Appreciative with jar mostly whole

indicators.note: most of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: to grate or jar is to irritate
full = whole, complete
FULL without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone is thankful to have a nearly full jar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jar' pretends to be a container; here it is the verb, to grate on the nerves.
explanation.definitionFit: Grateful and appreciative both mean thankful.

clue.text: Working on front of mirror's reflection

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter
in an across clue, written after the other piece

parts.note: first letter of mirror
working a machine is using it

explanation.surface: Someone works on the front of a mirror, perhaps polishing their reflection.
explanation.walkthrough: The mirror makes 'reflection' look like an image; it means thought.
explanation.definitionFit: Musing is thinking things over, which is reflection.

clue.text: Foundation perhaps complete

definitions.meaning: foundation is a cosmetic, and 'perhaps' marks it as one example of a wider class
as a two-word verb: to finish off the numbers or a set

explanation.walkthrough: 'Foundation' suggests a building's base; the 'perhaps' marks it as one example of cosmetics. The second sense is the verb, as in make up a team.
explanation.definitionFit: Foundation is one cosmetic among many, and to finish off a number or a set is to complete it.

clue.text: Joiner's feint pays off

indicators.note: off as in gone bad, so the letters are spoiled into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A carpenter's bluff works out for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joiner' suggests a carpenter; here it is anything that joins, and 'pays off' reads as a whole phrase until you split it.
explanation.definitionFit: A safety pin fastens two bits of fabric, so it is a joiner.

clue.text: Establishment deploying Polish to perfectly execute blockade?

parts.note: to nail a task is to do it perfectly
a bar blocks the way

explanation.surface: A military picture: Polish forces sent in to carry out a blockade.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P turns polish into Polish, suggesting troops from Poland. A nail bar is a salon where nails are painted.
explanation.definitionFit: A salon where manicurists paint on polish is an establishment that deploys it.

clue.text: Standard of college concerning queen's subordinate

parts.note: uni = university
a book on birds is concerning birds
in a pack of cards the jack ranks just below the queen

explanation.surface: A college rule about a queen's junior official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' reads as a benchmark; it is a flag. The Union Jack is the flag of the United Kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a flag, and the Union Jack is the British flag.

clue.text: Menial worker returns carrying one side dish

indicators.note: carrying means holding, so the reversed worker has the numeral inside it
returns means goes back, so the worker's letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a serf was a feudal labourer bound to the land, a menial worker
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A kitchen hand comes back to the table bearing a single side order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns SERF into FRES, which is 'carrying' I. 'returns' looks like the worker coming back with the dish, but it is a reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Fries, chips in Britain, are commonly served as an accompaniment to a main course.

clue.text: Pilot carrying key atomic weapon — on this?

definitions.text: Pilot carrying key atomic weapon — on this?

indicators.note: holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: to pilot is to steer
the Alt key on a keyboard
an H-bomb, a hydrogen bomb

explanation.surface: A pilot flying a nuclear weapon, and the question of what aircraft he is in.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also describes the aircraft itself, which is why it ends 'on this?'. Alt is a keyboard key; an H-bomb is a hydrogen bomb.
explanation.definitionFit: A stealth bomber is an aircraft built to carry bombs, including nuclear ones, undetected.

clue.text: Council erroneously holds back artefact

indicators.note: back means the hidden letters are read in reverse
holds means contains, so the answer's letters are found inside these words

parts.note: the letters CILER run across these two words

explanation.surface: A local council has wrongly kept hold of a historical object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' points to CILER inside Council erroneously, and 'back' reverses it. 'holds back' reads as withholds, but each word has its own job.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is an object surviving from an earlier time, a piece of history like an artefact.

clue.text: Fair in centre of city interrupting calm

indicators.note: takes the middle letters of city

parts.note: equable = even-tempered, calm

indicators.note: breaks into the other word, sitting inside it

parts.note: middle two letters of cITy, placed inside EQUABLE

explanation.surface: A fair held in the middle of town breaks the peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' pretends to be a funfair in the city centre; it is the adjective meaning just.
explanation.definitionFit: Equitable means fair and even-handed.

clue.text: Flower with head of carpel removed is flatter

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the buttercup is a yellow wild flower
first letter of carpel, removed from BUTTERCUP

explanation.surface: A botany note: a flower missing the top of its carpel is flatter.
explanation.walkthrough: The carpel is a real part of a flower, so the botany hangs together, and 'flatter' reads as less bumpy until it becomes the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To flatter someone is to lay on the praise, as if spreading it thick on bread.

clue.text: Spineless individual spoiled the marrow

indicators.note: ruined, so the letters are broken and rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A weakling ruined the prize vegetable, a marrow being a large courgette.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spineless individual' sounds like an insult for a coward; read literally, it is an animal with no backbone.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthworm is an invertebrate, literally a creature without a spine.

clue.text: Go round Paris, starting with entrance to Louvre

indicators.note: starting as in jumping up with a jolt, so the letters are jolted into a new order
the entrance to a word is its first letter

parts.note: anagram fodder
first letter of Louvre, added at the end

explanation.surface: Tourist advice: tour Paris, beginning at the Louvre's door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starting with' reads as 'beginning at', which suggests L comes first; in fact 'starting' is the anagram signal and L goes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving round and round in a widening curve is the verb sense of going round.

clue.text: Client dated study site of ancient civilization

parts.note: con is an old word meaning to study or learn by heart
Sumer, in ancient Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A customer went out with a student of an ancient civilization.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dated' looks like a verb, as in going out with someone; it marks CON as an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who buys goods or services is a client of the business.

clue.text: European secures leading choice

indicators.note: holds the other piece safely inside it

parts.note: a Serb is a European
up = ahead, as in two goals up; placed inside SERB

explanation.surface: A European wins the top pick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading choice' sounds like one noun phrase; 'choice' is the adjective, as in choice cuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Choice as an adjective means of top quality, superb.

clue.text: He painted image like so

definitions.note: 'He painted' stands for a noun: the man who painted

parts.note: pic = picture
as = like
used as it stands

explanation.surface: A painter produced a picture just like this.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole phrase 'He painted', meaning a man who painted.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo Picasso was one of the most famous painters.

clue.text: Do without king and church? Fantastic!

indicators.note: with the letter taken away

parts.note: a do is a hairdo, and a topknot is one
K = king in chess and cards, removed from TOPKNOT
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A republican cheer: manage without monarch and church? Brilliant!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do without' reads as one phrase meaning manage without; split it, 'Do' is a hairdo.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the highest quality, excellent: the informal sense of fantastic.

clue.text: Josh entertained by song for official

indicators.note: taken in as a guest, so it goes inside

parts.note: tune = song
to josh or rib someone is to tease them; placed inside TUNE

explanation.surface: A man named Josh is sung to on behalf of an official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Josh' looks like a name; it is the verb, to tease. A tribune was a Roman official.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribune was an official in ancient Rome elected to protect the people.

clue.text: Lord to get into line

parts.note: Cor! is a British exclamation of surprise, like Lord!
to don clothes is to get into them

explanation.surface: A nobleman is told to fall into line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lord' looks like a nobleman; it is the exclamation. Cor, from 'God', is everyday British slang for wow.
explanation.definitionFit: A cordon is a line of police or guards keeping people back.

clue.text: Colluding secretly with South American before riots

indicators.note: the first piece comes before the second

parts.note: the Inca people of Peru
a riot and a hoot are both very funny things or people

explanation.surface: A plot hatched with a South American ahead of civil unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riots' pushes towards disorder; it means laughs, as in 'the party was a riot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Working together secretly, as partners in a shady scheme, is colluding.

clue.text: Capital melody penned by company

indicators.note: shut in as if in a pen, so it goes inside

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
an air is a tune; placed inside CO

explanation.surface: A great tune written by a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' looks like an adjective meaning excellent, praising the melody; it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital city of Egypt, on the Nile.

clue.text: Class given role in a podcast

indicators.note: a podcast is listened to, so the word is heard rather than read and the spelling changes

parts.note: an actor given a role has been cast

explanation.surface: Someone of a particular social standing is given a part in an audio show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a podcast' looks like the location of the role, but it signals that CAST is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a hereditary social class, especially in the Hindu system, so a rank in society.

clue.text: Relish got us excited

indicators.note: stirred up, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters

explanation.surface: A condiment really got us going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relish' suggests a sauce, and the surface backs that up; it is the noun for enjoyment.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearty enjoyment, as in eating with zest, is relish.

clue.text: Let-down in Canada — MPs quibble

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words

parts.note: the letters spanning canaDA MPS QUIBble

explanation.surface: A political disappointment in Canada as its MPs argue over details.
explanation.walkthrough: A damp squib is a British phrase for a disappointing flop: a firework that fails to go off.
explanation.definitionFit: A firework that fizzles out instead of going bang is the image behind this anticlimax.

clue.text: Area accessible to the public seen regularly

definitions.meaning: open grassland in a British town or village that anyone may use

explanation.surface: A public area that you see all the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like a letter-picking signal; here it is plain meaning, often.
explanation.definitionFit: A common is shared public land, and something common is frequently seen.

clue.text: Creature unfortunately erred eating honey periodically

indicators.note: eating means taking in, so the rearranged letters hold the selected ones inside
unfortunately suggests things going wrong, so the letters of erred are rearranged
periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of honey

explanation.surface: An animal made a mistake by eating some honey now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges erred into RDEER, and 'periodically' takes OE from honey, which RDEER is 'eating' after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The roe deer is a small Eurasian deer, an animal and so a creature.
